name: Liam Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Liam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a working foreman for Brightwell, a small firm that does refurbs for the council: schools, the library, a couple of health centres. Right now we're in a primary school over the half-term break, so it's a mad rush to swap out thirty fire doors and put new partitions in two classrooms before the children come back on Monday. I start at seven, sort the crew into jobs, five of us plus Agnieszka, then I'm hanging doors myself till about five. Most evenings I'm also writing up the paperwork for the council at the kitchen table.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like old buildings. Nothing's square, every door frame is its own puzzle, and when you get a hundred-year-old door to close sweetly, that's a good feeling. What wears me out is the money side. The council gives the contract to whoever's cheapest, so Brightwell's always cutting corners on wages, and I earn less than foremen at the big firms. There aren't many of those round here, though, so I stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was a useful tool and that's all. I'd probably post something like, still need someone to hang the doors, turns out. Nobody at work would care much either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the same job and the same squeeze. I'd still be fighting the lowest-bid system, not the robots. Which is a fight I understand at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on. Keep using the AI thing for method statements because it saves me an hour some nights. Keep going to the union branch meeting once a month, and keep asking Brightwell's owner, Gareth, for the rise he keeps promising after the next contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. A bit relieved. Same tiredness as always, but nothing new to be scared of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI for the paperwork already. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I type in what we're doing, like replacing fire doors in a school corridor, and it gives me a first draft of the safety paperwork. I always have to fix it, it gets the regs wrong sometimes. But Priya says I'm in a better mood when I'm not up till eleven writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, does anything about your plans change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Priya and I want to save for a deposit one day, but on what we earn that's years off anyway. I've got maybe two and a half weeks of money in the account. AI fizzling out doesn't change that, sadly.

S0.say: I'd say fair enough, it was a useful tool and nothing more. Turns out you still need someone to hang the doors.
S0.think: It means the same job and the same squeeze. My fight is with the lowest-bid council contracts, not with robots, and at least I understand that fight.
S0.do: Carries on as foreman and keeps using AI for method statements to save an hour some evenings. Keeps attending the monthly union branch meeting and pressing his boss for a promised rise.
S0.feel: Calm and a little relieved, with the same old tiredness.
S0.quote: Priya says I'm in a better mood when I'm not up till eleven writing.
S0.fieldNote: Liam is already a light AI user, but only for paperwork, and he checks it. His frustration is aimed at how public contracts are awarded rather than at technology. His savings are so thin that even the calm picture leaves the house deposit years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the council needs to make sure the money saved goes back into training people. If firms save a fortune, workers should get some of it. I'd say that at the branch meeting and probably share a few articles about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm safer than most. Robots are good at new builds where everything's the same, but nothing in a 1930s school is the same. The paperwork side, the measuring, the ordering, that could go. But somebody still has to make that door fit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get better at the AI tools properly, maybe a short course if the union or the college has one, because the foreman who can do the planning fast keeps his job. I'd ask Gareth to put me on any new kit first. And I'd keep an eye on the jobs board in case the bigger firms start hiring people who can run the new stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit of background worry, but I can see a path through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your job do you think go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office side, probably. Quantities, ordering, scheduling. Maybe the surveying, with those scanners that map a room in a minute. The actual fitting in old buildings I think hangs on longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see what works. How long would you wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Until I see it working on a real job, not in a video. If Sean, our electrician, says a new tool saved him a day, I'd try it the next week. I'm not first in the queue, but I'm not last either.

S1.say: I'd say the council has to make sure money saved by AI goes back into training workers. If firms save a fortune, workers should get a share.
S1.think: I think I'm safer than most, because nothing in a 1930s school is the same and robots like sameness. The paperwork and measuring could go, but somebody still has to make the door fit.
S1.do: Learns the AI planning tools properly, ideally on a short union or college course, and asks to be first on any new kit. Watches the jobs board for bigger firms hiring people who can run new equipment.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with background worry but a visible path through.
S1.quote: Robots are good at new builds where everything's the same, but nothing in a 1930s school is the same.
S1.fieldNote: Liam reads his own safety in the awkwardness of old buildings, which is a thoughtful point. He is a classic second-wave adopter who waits for a colleague's word before trying something. He wants public money to follow any savings, in line with his politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to step in now, not in a year. Emergency support, a pause on firms sacking people until there's a plan. I'd be at the protest, and I'd be telling people not to blame each other, it's the companies selling these things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared. My old-buildings argument goes out the window if the robot can do anything a person can. And with two and a half weeks of money, I don't have time to work out a clever plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything we could and try to get a month or two of rent together. I'd push the union hard for a deal on redundancy pay and retraining. Once it arrives, I'd take whatever's going, maybe supervising the robots for Brightwell if they keep any of us, and if not, apply for any public support there is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I think I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym, the streaming, eating out. We'd stop going to Priya's sister's for weekends because the train costs forty each way. Christmas would be small. The car would be the hard one, I need it for work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lean on the union. What could they actually do in two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On their own, not much, to be honest. But together with nurses, teachers, drivers, all of us at once, that's a lot of votes. If it really hits everyone in two years, the government can't ignore that. That's the bit that gives me some hope.

S2.say: I'd say the government has to step in now with emergency support and a pause on sackings until there's a plan. I'd tell people not to blame each other but the companies selling this.
S2.think: I'd be scared, because my old-buildings argument is gone if a robot can do anything a person can. With two and a half weeks of money, there's no time for a clever plan.
S2.do: Cuts household spending to build a month or two of rent. Pushes the union for redundancy and retraining terms, then takes any robot-supervising role offered or applies for public support.
S2.quote: My old-buildings argument goes out the window if the robot can do anything a person can.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture removes the one advantage Liam had counted on. He shifts quickly to collective hope: if everyone is hit at once, the votes are there. His spending cuts are concrete, but he guards the car because the job needs it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's plan properly: public retraining, fair rules on who gets let go first. Less shouting, more getting it organised. I'd say that at work and at the branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is just about enough to get out ahead of it, if I start straight away. I'd hate to be the one who waited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sign up for a night course, probably building surveying or site management, something where you plan the job rather than do it. I'd keep putting thirty a week aside, which is all we can do. And I'd watch which firms bring in robots first and try to get a job with one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in control. Like a deadline at work, you know it's coming and you get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn, if you had the choice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Surveying, I think. You still need a person who understands why a building's falling apart and who can talk to a head teacher. Or running a crew of machines, if that's the job by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change anything between you and Priya?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. We'd talked about getting married in a couple of years and I'd want to hold off till I knew where I'd be. Priya might say that's silly, nurseries need people. She's probably right about her job, less sure about mine.

S3.say: I'd say we have a few years, so let's plan properly with public retraining and fair rules on who goes first. Less shouting, more organising.
S3.think: Five years is just about enough to get ahead of it, if I start straight away. I'd hate to be the one who waited.
S3.do: Signs up for a night course in building surveying or site management in the first year. Saves around 30 a week and aims to move to a firm that brings in robots early.
S3.feel: Anxious but in control, like a work deadline.
S3.quote: I'd hate to be the one who waited.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Liam turns from protest to planning, and pictures himself in surveying or crew management. He would hold off getting married until he knew where he stood, which he half thinks is silly. His savings target is small but honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the chance to do it right. Ten years is enough to train a whole generation differently, so there's no excuse. I'd probably say that loudly at the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be okay. I'm twenty-seven, I'm good at what I do, and ten years is time to get into surveying and have experience before the machines catch up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running jobs for Brightwell for a couple of years while I watch how fast it moves. Then around year two or three I'd do the surveying course and look for a trainee role. And I'd push the union to set up proper courses for everyone, not just the ones with time on their hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's still a big thing, but it's far enough off that I'd mostly just get on with life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Would you actually start in the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, to be honest. I'd watch first. That's how I am, I want to see the new tool work before I buy it. With ten years I'd tell myself I've got time, and maybe that's a mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Agnieszka and the others on your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Agnieszka is brilliant but her English reading isn't great, so any course with a lot of written tests would shut her out. I'd want the union to sort that. She can fit a door frame faster than me and she deserves a shot too.

S4.say: I'd say this is the chance to do it right, because ten years is enough to train a generation differently. There's no excuse to leave anyone behind.
S4.think: Privately, I think I'd be okay. At twenty-seven, with ten years, I can get into surveying and build experience before the machines catch up.
S4.do: Keeps working for Brightwell for a couple of years while watching the pace of change. Takes a surveying course around year two or three and presses the union to run courses open to everyone.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but far enough off to get on with life.
S4.quote: She can fit a door frame faster than me and she deserves a shot too.
S4.fieldNote: The extra time makes Liam slower to act, and he admits that might be a mistake. His concern for a colleague whose reading would shut her out of courses shows his progressive values in a practical form. He sees his age as an advantage here.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. There's just no time to do anything except panic and cut back. What would help is the government paying for retraining while you're still in work, evenings and weekends, so you don't have to quit to learn. And some rule that firms can't just let people go overnight.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe the council. Everyone talks about the big firms, but loads of building work is public money. If the council decided to keep people on its jobs, that would matter round here more than anything a tech company says.

headlineQuote: If the council decided to keep people on its jobs, that would matter round here more than anything a tech company says.
portrait: Liam is a 27-year-old working foreman for a small firm refurbishing council schools and buildings, living with his partner Priya, a nursery teacher, above a bakery on about two and a half weeks of savings. He uses AI now and then for safety paperwork and adopts new tools once a colleague says they work. He believes old buildings protect him from robots in the slower pictures, but that hope collapses with AGI in two years, when he is alarmed and turns to collective action. With five or ten years he plans to move into surveying, though with a decade he admits he would probably wait too long to start.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there would be no time to do anything except panic and cut back.
whatWouldHelp: Government-paid retraining he can do in the evenings while still working, a rule stopping firms letting people go overnight, and councils choosing to keep people on public jobs.
